transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

My sleep has been all over the place for weeks, and I can’t seem to get any real rest no matter how exhausted I feel. It has gotten to the point where I'm just constantly drained, and I really need some help figuring out why I can't recover.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling sad, empty, or hopeless, along with your sleep disturbances?

Yes, my mood has definitely taken a turn along with my sleep. Lately, it feels like someone turned the color down on my whole life, and I walk around feeling hollow and on the verge of tears for no clear reason. There is just this heavy sadness sitting in my chest that I can't seem to shake.

Have you experienced episodes like this before, where your mood and sleep were affected for a period, and then you returned to feeling normal, or has this been a persistent feeling that's been worsening over time?

These cycles of getting highly energetic and productive, and then crashing into long, dark lows, have been happening on and off for about a year since my husband's heart problems worsened. This heavy, low feeling has hung over me for most of the year, only interrupted by brief, intense spells of feeling wired and driven before I sink back down again.
Can you tell me more about the duration of these 'wired and driven' spells, how long they typically last, and how they differ from your normal self?

Those wired spells usually last for about a week and are completely different from my normal, structured self. During them, I only sleep three or four hours a night but feel incredibly energized, talking a mile a minute, snapping at people, and impulsively spending money on massive projects. These intense phases, followed by the deep crashes, have been happening on and off for about a year now.

Can you describe how your thoughts and behaviors are during these 'wired and driven' spells, specifically if you experience any racing thoughts, distractibility, or engage in risky behaviors that you later regret?

During those spells, my mind is absolutely buzzing with ideas and I talk a mile a minute, starting multiple projects at once like reorganizing clinic supply cabinets or planning elaborate trips. I also make risky choices I later regret, like driving too fast and aggressively between appointments or impulsively spending money we don't really have on expensive garden equipment and bird feeders.

Can you clarify if these episodes of feeling 'wired and driven' and the subsequent lows have been occurring in a pattern that resembles a clear cycle, with each episode lasting a specific amount of time, or if they seem more irregular and unpredictable?

Yes, there is a clear pattern of cycles that started about a year ago. The low, depressed periods are much longer and heavier, with this current one dragging on for almost the entire year, while the 'wired' high phases are much shorter, usually only lasting about a week before I crash back down.

Can you estimate how many of these cycles of high and low episodes you've experienced in the past year, and do you feel like the duration or intensity of either the highs or lows has changed over time?

I don't have an exact count, but the heavy, depressed feelings have dominated most of the past year, only interrupted a few times by those brief, week-long wired stretches. It definitely feels like the lows are lasting longer and becoming much harder to shake off. These cycles have been happening on and off ever since my husband's heart issues escalated a year ago.

Can you tell me if the duration of your depressive episodes has been consistently longer than your manic or hypomanic episodes, and have you noticed any seasonal pattern or specific triggers that seem to precede these episodes?

Yes, the depressive periods are definitely much longer, as this current heavy low has lasted for close to a year with only those brief, week-long breaks of feeling wired. I haven't noticed any seasonal pattern, but the clear trigger is my husband's worsening heart condition and the constant stress and sleep deprivation of caring for him.
Have you experienced any episodes of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted less than 4 consecutive days, or have all your 'wired and driven' spells lasted around a week as you mentioned?
No, I don't recall ever having those wired spells last less than four days. The ones I can remember, like the recent one, have consistently lasted for about a week.

Have you ever experienced a period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted at least 4 consecutive days but less than 7 days, or have all your elevated mood episodes consistently lasted around a week?

That recent elevated phase definitely lasted for about a week, and during that time I was only sleeping three or four hours a night. I'm not completely sure if I've had shorter stretches of four to six days, but that week-long period is the one that really stands out to me.

Can you confirm whether you have experienced any episodes of elevated mood that lasted at least 4 consecutive days but less than 7 days, which might be distinct from the week-long episodes you've described?

I'm really not sure if I've had other specific episodes that lasted between four and six days. I haven't tracked my moods closely enough to distinguish that, and I only recall those main high periods lasting about a week.

Can you try to recall or estimate if there have been any instances where you felt abnormally elevated or irritable for at least 4 days but less than a week, separate from the week-long episodes you've mentioned, even if they seem less significant or memorable?

Looking back over the past year, I actually have had some of those shorter spells lasting several days where I felt abnormally wired, upbeat, and irritable. During those times, I felt incredibly driven, needed very little sleep, and would snap at people, but I just brushed them off as highly productive phases rather than a medical issue. These high-energy periods typically lasted anywhere from several days to about a week.

Can you distinguish between episodes of elevated mood that lasted at least 4 consecutive days but less than 7 days, and those that lasted around a week, in terms of their impact on your daily functioning and relationships?

I can't really distinguish between episodes of those specific lengths because I haven't tracked my moods that precisely. When I get revved up, it just feels like one continuous blur of high energy that lasts around a week or so. It is really hard for me to separate the impacts on my life based on just a few days' difference.

Can you try to recall if the shorter elevated mood episodes, lasting between 4 to 6 days, had a significant impact on your daily life, relationships, or work, similar to the week-long episodes you described?

I'm not quite sure because I haven't really tracked the difference between a four-to-six-day stretch and a week-long one. They all just blend together into the same overwhelming cycle of highs and lows that I've been dealing with over the past year. It is really hard for me to separate how they impacted my life based on just a couple of days' difference.

Can you think of any instances where these shorter elevated mood episodes, lasting less than a week, caused significant problems in your relationships, work, or daily activities, similar to the longer episodes?

Yes, during those shorter, revved-up phases that lasted about a week, I definitely caused some real problems, like spending way too much money online on expensive garden equipment and bird feeders without checking our budget. I also drove too fast and aggressively between my husband's appointments because I constantly felt so rushed. Overall, these intense swings have really strained my relationships with my friends and just added to the general chaos of my life.
Can you confirm if any of your elevated mood episodes, regardless of their impact, lasted at least 4 consecutive days but less than 7 days, which could help clarify the nature of your condition?

Yes, I can confirm that those high phases where I felt oddly upbeat and barely slept typically lasted for about a week—usually right around four to seven days—before I crashed back down into depression. While it's hard to pinpoint the exact number of days for every single time, they consistently fell into that four-to-seven-day range.
Can you confirm if any of your elevated mood episodes lasted at least 4 consecutive days but less than 7 days, which could help clarify the nature of your condition?

Yes, I can confirm that. Those high, revved-up phases where I felt so upbeat and barely slept typically lasted right around four to seven days before I crashed back down into a low mood. It was almost always that week-long range.

Can you confirm if all your elevated mood episodes, which lasted at least 4 consecutive days, consistently met the full criteria for a manic episode, including significant impairment in social or occupational functioning or requiring hospitalization, or if they were more characteristic of hypomanic episodes with less severe impairment?

They were definitely more like hypomanic episodes, as I was never hospitalized and mostly felt highly productive, wired, and slept very little during those times. While I did make some impulsive decisions like overspending, the severe mistakes at work and real impairment mostly hit me during the exhaustion of the crashes. It's the overall instability of the swings, rather than the high phases themselves being completely disabling, that has caused the most trouble.

Can you confirm whether the functional impairment or distress caused by your elevated mood episodes was significant enough to warrant hospitalization or cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, which could help differentiate between manic and hypomanic episodes?

No, I have never been hospitalized during those high periods, and I wasn't out of touch with reality, even though I did get extremely driven, spent too much money, and drove a bit recklessly. The severe impairment—like my formal write-ups at the clinic for imaging errors, skipping my own medical care, and pulling away from friends—mostly happens because of the constant, exhausting swings and the deep crashes that follow those high stretches.

Can you confirm whether the episodes of elevated mood that lasted at least 4 consecutive days but less than 7 days caused significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning, or were they more characteristic of hypomanic episodes with less severe impairment?

Yes, those high phases were definitely more like hypomanic episodes where I felt incredibly wired and highly productive rather than severely impaired on their own. During those times, I felt like I was getting a ton done, sleeping very little, and taking on all sorts of clinic and home projects. The actual impairment, like my write-ups at work and withdrawing from friends, really only hit me when I crashed into those deep, exhausted lows.

Can you confirm whether any of your elevated mood episodes, lasting at least 4 consecutive days, were severe enough to cause significant impairment in social or occupational functioning or require hospitalization, which could help differentiate between a manic episode and a hypomanic episode?

Those high, wired phases usually lasted about a week, and I have never been hospitalized for them. During those times, I actually felt unusually productive, energized, and capable of taking on extra projects, even though I made some impulsive purchases and drove too fast. The severe impairment, like my formal write-ups at work, only happens when I crash into the low, exhausted periods rather than during the high phases themselves.

Yes, those episodes were definitely more hypomanic. I actually felt highly productive, driven, and capable at work, even though I was irritable and made some impulsive purchases. The severe impairment, like my clinic write-ups and withdrawing from friends, only happened when I crashed into my deep depressions.

I can confirm they were hypomanic and didn't cause severe impairment on their own; in fact, during those phases I felt unusually driven and highly productive, taking on extra projects at the clinic despite some impulsive spending and fast driving. The actual severe impairment, like my costly mistakes on radiographs, neglecting my own health, and pulling away from friends, only happened when I crashed into those low, exhausted periods.

Yes, those elevated periods of about a week were hypomanic; I felt like I was functioning on overdrive, taking on extra projects and staying up late without feeling severely impaired at the time. The severe impairment, like my major mistakes at the clinic and pulling away from friends, only hits me during the exhausting crashes. It is really the overall instability of these constant swings that has disrupted my life.

No, I have never been hospitalized for those high periods, even though I did some risky things like driving too fast and spending too much on garden equipment during those revved-up weeks. The severe impairment, like my formal write-ups at the clinic and pulling away from friends, mostly happens during the crashes or from the overall chaotic swings rather than the highs themselves.

To confirm, you're saying that during these high, wired phases, you felt highly productive and driven, but the significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning, such as mistakes at work or pulling away from friends, primarily occurred during the low, exhausted periods rather than the high phases themselves, is that correct?

Yes, that is exactly right. While I did some impulsive things during those high phases, like overspending on garden gear and driving too fast, I felt highly productive at the time. The actual breakdown in my ability to function—such as making mistakes on radiographs, getting formal write-ups at the clinic, and pulling away from my running club and friends—only happened when I crashed into those low, exhausted periods.
